14	# Strength Expression Depends on Torque Management, Not Just Load
15	
16	**What it is** — Torque (force times the perpendicular distance from the force's line of
17	action to the joint fulcrum) determines effective loading on a joint, independent of the
18	absolute weight lifted. Bringing a load closer to a joint reduces the torque at that
19	joint for the same weight: flexing the elbows reduces shoulder torque during dumbbell
20	raises/flyes/bench press; keeping a bar close to the body during the clean or deadlift
21	reduces torque at the lumbar spine and hips, allowing a heavier load to be lifted more
22	safely. Swinging the bar away from the body during a snatch pull, or a javelin away from
23	the shoulder during wind-up, are cited as inefficient uses of torque. (PDF pp. 28-29,
24	printed pp. 17-18.)
25	
26	**Why it works** — Torque = force x moment arm; for a fixed external force (a given
27	weight), shortening the moment arm directly lowers the rotational demand on the joint,
28	which is standard, independently-established biomechanics, not specific to this text.
29	
30	**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a coaching cue and technical-fault-diagnosis
31	tool for any lift where the bar or load can drift away from the body's midline (clean,
32	snatch, deadlift, overhead press) or away from a joint (dumbbell raises, flyes); keeping
33	the load's path close to the relevant joint is both a safety cue and a load-capacity cue.
34	This general coaching application is this entry's own extension of Verkhoshansky's
35	worked examples (PDF pp. 28-29, printed pp. 17-18).
36	
37	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a mechanical principle about joint
38	loading, not a complete safety framework; it does not account for tissue tolerance,
39	technique proficiency, or fatigue-related form breakdown on its own, and the text does
40	not claim that it does. **Inference:** reducing joint torque is not always desirable if
41	the goal is specifically to overload that joint's musculature for rehabilitation purposes
42	(e.g., some hip- or shoulder-isolation rehab work intentionally increases moment arm at a
43	target joint under controlled load); this rehab caveat is not addressed in this section of
44	the text.
45	
46	**Example** — **Inference:** Cueing an athlete to keep the bar against the shins and thighs during a
47	clean pull, rather than swinging it forward, reduces lumbar torque for the same bar
48	weight and is both a technique and a load-management fix.
49

# The Muscle Model: Series Elastic Component (SEC) vs. Parallel Elastic Component (PEC)

**What it is** — A mechanical model of muscle (Levin & Wyman, 1927) treats it as a
contractile component in series with a Series Elastic Component (SEC: tendon,
cross-bridges, myofilaments, titin, Z-discs) and in parallel with a Parallel Elastic
Component (PEC: sarcolemma, rest-state cross-bridging, surrounding sheaths). The PEC
carries the force of a relaxed muscle stretched beyond resting length, and stores little
usable energy; the SEC is tensioned by an actively contracting muscle resisting a rapid
stretch, and stores considerable elastic energy (this is the mechanism plyometric/shock
training exploits). Slow-twitch (ST) dominant muscle shows smaller mechanical strain when
stretched while contracted but has a stiffer, more elastic SEC than fast-twitch
(FT)-dominant muscle, largely due to higher collagen concentration in slow muscle. The book
gives conflicting statements on which fibre type stores more elastic energy overall:
printed 41 states "the stored elastic energy is greater in FT fibres" (Komi, 1984), while
printed 46 states "a slow muscle can store relatively more elastic energy in its
collagenous tissue than fast muscle." Both are recorded here rather than harmonized.
Static, relaxed, and passive stretching mainly load the PEC; "tense ballistic and active
stretching affects predominantly the SEC," while PNF techniques "appear to be able to
stretch and strengthen both the SEC and the PEC" (printed 41-42). (PDF pp. 51-53, 57;
printed pp. 40-42, 46.)

**Why it works** — Inference: knowing which component (PEC or SEC) is under tension in a
given stretch or contraction explains why static/passive and active/PNF stretching target
different tissue; the book conflicts on which fibre type stores more elastic energy
(printed 41 vs. 46), so no single fibre-type/component pairing can be asserted as the
mechanism.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful for explaining why plyometric/reactive-strength
training targets the SEC specifically (rapid stretch under active contraction) rather than
simple static flexibility work (which mostly loads the PEC), and for choosing PNF-style
active stretching when the goal is to influence both components rather than the PEC alone.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the anatomical location of SEC/PEC elements is
explicitly stated as not precisely identified (PDF p. 52, printed p. 41); treat this as a
functional/mechanical model for reasoning about elastic energy, not a literal anatomical
map to test or measure directly in an athlete.

**Example** — Inference: by the authors' own account, slow postural muscle needs longer
stretching to meaningfully change its flexibility than fast muscle does (printed 41), which
supports muscle-specific rather than uniform flexibility prescription; this is distinct
from, and does not depend on, the unresolved FT-vs-ST elastic-energy-storage conflict
above.

**Related** — [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]],
[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]].

# Four Features of the Adaptation Process: Overload, Accommodation, Specificity, Individualization

**What it is** — The authors give a four-item checklist that "from a practical point of
view" governs sport training adaptation: (1) stimulus magnitude (overload), (2)
accommodation, (3) specificity, and (4) individualization (printed p. 4). **Overload**: a
training adaptation happens only if the training load is above the athlete's habitual
level, achieved either by raising intensity/volume on the same drill or by switching to a
new, unaccustomed drill. Below-habitual load causes detraining. Training loads are
classified as stimulating (above the neutral zone, drives adaptation), retaining (within
the neutral zone, maintains fitness), or detraining (below it) (figure 1.1). Elite
athletes' training load is roughly 10 times that of beginners with 6 months' experience:
elite weightlifters lift around 5,000 tons/year versus 1/10th-1/12th of that for novices;
elite cross-country skiers cover 8,000-12,000 km/year versus about 1,000 km for beginners
(printed pp. 4-5). **Accommodation** and **specificity** are each large enough topics to
carry their own entries in this library ([[principle--accommodation-and-the-diminishing-returns-law]],
[[framework--transfer-of-training-coefficient-calculation]]). **Individualization**:
"training programs must be adjusted individually to each athlete. Remember that all
people are different" (printed p. 15) — stated here only as a checklist item, not
developed further in this chapter. (PDF pp. 13-15, printed pp. 4-5, 15.)

**Why it works** — Inference: the authors do not give a unified mechanism for why these
four features specifically govern adaptation; each is instead grounded separately in its
own subsection (overload in the dose-response and detraining discussion, accommodation in
a biological-response-decay argument, specificity in the transfer-of-training data,
individualization only asserted). Treat this entry's "why it works" as a summary of the
book's own separate justifications, not a single mechanism.

**When to apply** — As a four-point programming checklist when auditing whether a training
block is actually driving adaptation: is the load above the athlete's habitual level
(overload), is it varied enough to avoid accommodation, is it close enough to the target
skill to transfer (specificity), and is it adjusted to this athlete rather than copied from
a template (individualization). **Eric's baseline:** individualization matches Baylor's own
department framing that stressors are additive and load must be adjusted per athlete
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power" and the vault's own
[[periodization--bompa/principle--individualization]], which already treats
individualization in full depth); this entry does not add a new angle on individualization
beyond restating the checklist item, so readers wanting the developed treatment should use
the Bompa entry.

**When NOT to apply** — Inference: the elite-vs-beginner load ratios (10x, 5,000 tons/yr,
8,000-12,000 km/yr) are illustrative benchmarks from weightlifting and cross-country
skiing, not a football-specific dosing rule; do not transfer them directly to a
position-group's off-season volume without adjustment. The individualization item is
asserted, not developed with a mechanism or example in this chapter; do not treat it as
carrying independent evidentiary weight here.

**Example** — The training-load classification is illustrated with identical triplets: all
three could lift a 57.5-kg barbell once; they began training with a 50-kg barbell to
failure at 5 reps; once adapted, they could lift 60 kg once but stopped improving further
on the same routine. At that point Athlete A increased the load (stimulating load,
improved further), Athlete B kept the same routine (retaining load, no change), and
Athlete C decreased the load (detraining load, strength declined) (printed p. 5, the
authors' own example, not invented).

**Related** — [[principle--accommodation-and-the-diminishing-returns-law]],
[[framework--transfer-of-training-coefficient-calculation]],
[[periodization--bompa/principle--individualization]] (fuller treatment of
individualization), [[periodization--bompa/principle--progressive-overload-threshold]]
(fuller treatment of overload).

# Accommodation: Why a Fixed Exercise and Load Stop Producing Gains

**What it is** — If an athlete uses the same exercise at the same training load over a
long period, performance improvement decreases; the authors call this **accommodation**,
"a manifestation... often considered a general law of biology": the response of a
biological object to a constant stimulus decreases over time. In training, the stimulus is
physical exercise and the response is performance improvement; with increasing training
volume or duration the magnitude of adaptation diminishes, which the authors name the
**principle of diminishing returns** (printed p. 5). Their own illustration: "A Bizarre
Bank Metaphor" — imagine a bank that pays a smaller interest rate the longer money stays
deposited and the larger the deposit, the opposite of ordinary banking; "this is exactly
how our body works," and a real bank with that policy would go out of business (printed p.
6, the authors' own analogy). Programs are modified two ways to avoid accommodation:
quantitatively (changing training loads, e.g. total weight lifted) or qualitatively
(replacing exercises); the text credits elite track and field athletes who avoided
accommodation across three consecutive Olympic Games by varying drills year to year, for
instance using an efficient drill (overhead throwing of a 3-kg shot by a javelin thrower)
only during an Olympic season or once in a 4-year period (printed p. 6). Training programs
face a stated conflict: they must be **variable**, to avoid accommodation, while also
being **stable/specific**, to satisfy the demand for transfer, since the highest transfer
of training occurs with sport-specific exercises (printed p. 6; see
[[framework--transfer-of-training-coefficient-calculation]]). (PDF pp. 14-15, printed pp.
5-6.)

**Why it works** — The authors give the mechanism only at the level of "a general law of
biology" (a constant stimulus produces a decreasing biological response over time); they
do not name a specific physiological pathway (e.g. receptor down-regulation, neural
habituation) for why training accommodation specifically occurs. Inference: this is
consistent with the same diminishing-marginal-adaptation logic that shows up elsewhere in
exercise science under different names (e.g. detraining thresholds, novelty effects in
motor learning), but the authors do not draw that connection themselves.

**When to apply** — As the stated rationale for periodized variation: rotate exercises or
load qualitatively/quantitatively once gains from a given routine plateau, rather than
running the same protocol indefinitely. **Eric's baseline:** in-season programming
deliberately waves volume and intensity even when the practice schedule looks repetitive,
"specifically to avoid training monotony for the athlete" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Periodization and programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.21`).
Inference: this is the same accommodation logic Zatsiorsky and Kraemer describe, applied
to in-season football; the baseline material does not itself use the term
"accommodation."

**When NOT to apply** — The Olympic-cycle example (varying a drill's frequency across a
4-year cycle) is a coaching anecdote, not a controlled comparison; the authors do not
report data isolating accommodation from other seasonal factors (competition taper,
maturation, other training changes) in that example. Inference: the variable-vs-specific
tension the authors name is a real constraint, not a rule that resolves in one direction;
do not use "avoid accommodation" alone to justify replacing sport-specific exercises with
novel ones at the expense of transfer.

**Example** — The authors' own worked example: identical triplets with equal starting
strength trained with the same 50-kg barbell to failure; once adapted and able to lift 60
kg, further gains stopped on the unchanged routine (accommodation) until the load or
exercise was changed (see [[framework--four-features-of-the-adaptation-process]] for the
full triplet example with all three athletes' outcomes).

**Related** — [[framework--four-features-of-the-adaptation-process]],
[[framework--transfer-of-training-coefficient-calculation]],
[[periodization--bompa/principle--progressive-overload-threshold]].

# Accommodation: Why a Fixed Exercise and Load Stop Producing Gains

**What it is** — If an athlete uses the same exercise at the same training load over a
long period, performance improvement decreases; the authors call this **accommodation**,
"a manifestation... often considered a general law of biology": the response of a
biological object to a constant stimulus decreases over time. In training, the stimulus is
physical exercise and the response is performance improvement; with increasing training
volume or duration the magnitude of adaptation diminishes, which the authors name the
**principle of diminishing returns** (printed p. 5). Their own illustration: "A Bizarre
Bank Metaphor" — imagine a bank that pays a smaller interest rate the longer money stays
deposited and the larger the deposit, the opposite of ordinary banking; "this is exactly
how our body works," and a real bank with that policy would go out of business (printed p.
6, the authors' own analogy). Programs are modified two ways to avoid accommodation:
quantitatively (changing training loads, e.g. total weight lifted) or qualitatively
(replacing exercises); the text credits elite track and field athletes who avoided
accommodation across three consecutive Olympic Games by varying drills year to year, for
instance using an efficient drill (overhead throwing of a 3-kg shot by a javelin thrower)
only during an Olympic season or once in a 4-year period (printed p. 6). Training programs
face a stated conflict: they must be **variable**, to avoid accommodation, while also
being **stable/specific**, to satisfy the demand for transfer, since the highest transfer
of training occurs with sport-specific exercises (printed p. 6; see
[[framework--transfer-of-training-coefficient-calculation]]). (PDF pp. 14-15, printed pp.
5-6.)

**Why it works** — The authors give the mechanism only at the level of "a general law of
biology" (a constant stimulus produces a decreasing biological response over time); they
do not name a specific physiological pathway (e.g. receptor down-regulation, neural
habituation) for why training accommodation specifically occurs. Inference: this is
consistent with the same diminishing-marginal-adaptation logic that shows up elsewhere in
exercise science under different names (e.g. detraining thresholds, novelty effects in
motor learning), but the authors do not draw that connection themselves.

load qualitatively/quantitatively once gains from a given routine plateau, rather than
running the same protocol indefinitely. **Eric's baseline:** in-season programming
deliberately waves volume and intensity even when the practice schedule looks repetitive,

to in-season football; the baseline material does not itself use the term

# Calculating a Transfer-of-Training Coefficient from Effect Size

**What it is** — The authors give a stepwise method to quantify how much an exercise's
gains carry over to a different, untrained task. Because performances in different
exercises have different units (force, time, distance) and are not directly comparable,
they use a dimensionless unit, **result gain**, expressed in standard deviations: result
gain = gain of performance / standard deviation of performance (equivalent to what the
text separately calls "effect size": [post-training mean − pretraining mean] / pretraining
SD). The **transfer coefficient** is then: transfer = result gain in the nontrained
exercise / result gain in the trained exercise. The higher the ratio, the greater the
transfer (printed pp. 8-9). The method is demonstrated with a real dataset (Zatsiorsky and
Raitsin, 1974): two groups trained isometric knee extension at a fixed joint angle (Group
1: 70°; Group 2: 130°), then both were tested on force at that angle and on barbell squat
performance. Group 1: force gain 410 ± 170 N (result gain 410/340 = 1.2), squat gain 11.5 ±
5.4 kg (result gain 11.5/23 = 0.5), transfer = 0.5/1.2 = **0.42**. Group 2: force gain 560 ±
230 N (result gain 560/618 = 0.91), squat gain 7.5 ± 4.7 kg (result gain 7.5/28 = 0.27),
transfer = 0.27/0.91 = **0.30**. Despite Group 2 showing the larger absolute force gain
(560 vs. 410 N) and the larger absolute squat gain (11.5 ± 5.4 vs. 7.5 ± 4.7 kg went to
Group 1, not Group 2 — Group 1 actually had the larger squat kg gain), Group 1's training
method produced the higher transfer coefficient (0.42 vs. 0.30) and is judged to have
better improved squat performance because of higher transfer, not higher trained-exercise
gain (printed p. 9, table "Calculating the Transfer of Training Results"). (PDF pp. 16-18,
printed pp. 7-9; data from Zatsiorsky, V.M. and Raitsin, L.M., 1974, "Transfer of
cumulative training effects in strength exercises," Theory and Practice of Physical
Culture 6: 7-14.)

**Why it works** — Inference: normalizing by each exercise's own population standard
deviation controls for the fact that different tests have different natural variability
and different units, so a raw kg or N gain cannot be compared directly across exercises;
expressing both the trained and untrained gain in the same SD-based unit before taking
their ratio is what makes the transfer coefficient comparable across different exercise
pairs and studies. The authors state this reasoning directly (printed p. 9) rather than
leaving it as this entry's inference.

**When to apply** — As a field-usable method for comparing two training methods' carryover
to a target lift or skill, when pre/post data with means and SDs exist for both the trained
exercise and the target task: compute each result gain (post-pre / pretraining SD), then
divide the nontrained-exercise result gain by the trained-exercise result gain. **Eric's
baseline:** Applied Performance already reports force-plate metrics against an
Output/Driver/Strategy framework rather than raw values alone (`method-baseline.md`,
"Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing `hd-odsf-metrics.md`); Inference: this
transfer-coefficient method is a compatible, more rigorous complement for specifically
answering "did this training method transfer," which the ODSF framework does not itself
address.

**When NOT to apply** — This single study (two groups, isometric knee extension at 70° vs.
130°, squat as the transfer target) is Soviet-era, single-lab evidence; confidence is
capped at `supported`, not `proven`. Inference: do not treat 0.42 or 0.30 as universal
transfer benchmarks for other exercise pairs; the coefficient is specific to this exercise
pair, this joint angle manipulation, and this population, and would need to be recomputed
for a different training method or target lift. The method also requires a defined trained
exercise and a defined target/nontrained exercise measured before and after; it cannot be
computed retroactively without pretraining SD data.

**Example** — Beyond the isometric-angle study above, the authors' own conceptual example:
young athletes trained on squats (exercise A) improve 20 kg on average; the same training's
carryover to standing vertical jump, sprint dash, or freestyle swimming (exercises B, C, D)
would differ, plausibly substantial in the vertical jump, small in sprinting, and "next to
nothing" in swimming (printed p. 6) — the authors' own prediction, not this entry's
invention, though no transfer coefficients are computed for that specific triad in the
text.

**Related** — [[framework--four-features-of-the-adaptation-process]],
[[principle--accommodation-and-the-diminishing-returns-law]],
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (a
later, qualitative ten-dimension taxonomy of the same specificity/transfer problem this
quantitative method measures).

# Calculating a Transfer-of-Training Coefficient from Effect Size

**What it is** — The authors give a stepwise method to quantify how much an exercise's
gains carry over to a different, untrained task. Because performances in different
exercises have different units (force, time, distance) and are not directly comparable,
they use a dimensionless unit, **result gain**, expressed in standard deviations: result
gain = gain of performance / standard deviation of performance (equivalent to what the
text separately calls "effect size": [post-training mean − pretraining mean] / pretraining
SD). The **transfer coefficient** is then: transfer = result gain in the nontrained
exercise / result gain in the trained exercise. The higher the ratio, the greater the
transfer (printed pp. 8-9). The method is demonstrated with a real dataset (Zatsiorsky and
Raitsin, 1974): two groups trained isometric knee extension at a fixed joint angle (Group
1: 70°; Group 2: 130°), then both were tested on force at that angle and on barbell squat
performance. Group 1: force gain 410 ± 170 N (result gain 410/340 = 1.2), squat gain 11.5 ±
5.4 kg (result gain 11.5/23 = 0.5), transfer = 0.5/1.2 = **0.42**. Group 2: force gain 560 ±
230 N (result gain 560/618 = 0.91), squat gain 7.5 ± 4.7 kg (result gain 7.5/28 = 0.27),
transfer = 0.27/0.91 = **0.30**. The results table (printed p. 9) shows a deliberate
contrast: Group 2 had the larger absolute force gain in the trained exercise (560 ± 230 vs.
410 ± 170 N) and the larger result gain there (1.2 vs. 0.91 SD went to Group 1 instead —
Group 1's trained-exercise result gain, 1.2 SD, was actually the higher of the two), yet
Group 1 had the larger squat-kg gain (11.5 ± 5.4 vs. 7.5 ± 4.7 kg) and the higher transfer
coefficient (0.42 vs. 0.30). The authors' conclusion: "because of the higher transfer of
training results, the method used to train the first group better improved the squatting
performance" (printed p. 9) — transfer coefficient, not raw trained-exercise gain, is what
predicted the better outcome on the untrained target exercise. (PDF pp. 16-18,
printed pp. 7-9; data from Zatsiorsky, V.M. and Raitsin, L.M., 1974, "Transfer of
cumulative training effects in strength exercises," Theory and Practice of Physical
Culture 6: 7-14.)

**Why it works** — Inference: normalizing by each exercise's own population standard
deviation controls for the fact that different tests have different natural variability
and different units, so a raw kg or N gain cannot be compared directly across exercises;
expressing both the trained and untrained gain in the same SD-based unit before taking
their ratio is what makes the transfer coefficient comparable across different exercise
pairs and studies. The authors state this reasoning directly (printed p. 9) rather than
leaving it as this entry's inference.

**When to apply** — As a field-usable method for comparing two training methods' carryover
to a target lift or skill, when pre/post data with means and SDs exist for both the trained
exercise and the target task: compute each result gain (post-pre / pretraining SD), then
divide the nontrained-exercise result gain by the trained-exercise result gain. **Eric's
baseline:** Applied Performance already reports force-plate metrics against an
Output/Driver/Strategy framework rather than raw values alone (`method-baseline.md`,
"Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing `hd-odsf-metrics.md`); Inference: this
transfer-coefficient method is a compatible, more rigorous complement for specifically
answering "did this training method transfer," which the ODSF framework does not itself
address.

**When NOT to apply** — This single study (two groups, isometric knee extension at 70° vs.
130°, squat as the transfer target) is Soviet-era, single-lab evidence; confidence is
capped at `supported`, not `proven`. Inference: do not treat 0.42 or 0.30 as universal
transfer benchmarks for other exercise pairs; the coefficient is specific to this exercise
pair, this joint angle manipulation, and this population, and would need to be recomputed
for a different training method or target lift. The method also requires a defined trained
exercise and a defined target/nontrained exercise measured before and after; it cannot be
computed retroactively without pretraining SD data.

young athletes trained on squats (exercise A) improve 20 kg on average; the same training's

text.

# The One-Factor (Supercompensation) Theory, and the Authors' Own Critique of It

**What it is** — The **one-factor theory** (supercompensation theory) holds that the
immediate effect of a workout is a depletion of certain biochemical substances; after the
restoration period the level of the substance rises above its initial level
(supercompensation), and if the next workout lands during that supercompensation phase,
preparedness increases (figure 1.4). If rest intervals are too short, preparedness
decreases from accumulated fatigue (figure 1.5a); if optimal, workouts land in the
supercompensation phase (1.5b); if too long, there is no stable training effect (1.5c).
Coaches sometimes stack several short-interval, high-load sessions (accumulating fatigue on
purpose) followed by one longer rest, the "overloading microcycle," on the belief this
produces supercompensation greater than normal (figure 1.6) — the authors call this only "a
common belief," not a demonstrated result. Then, directly, the authors' own critique
(printed p. 12): "The very existence of the supercompensation phase for a majority of
metabolic substances has never been experimentally proven." Muscle glycogen supercompensation
specifically has been demonstrated and can be induced with a training-plus-carbohydrate-
loading protocol, but that procedure "cannot be reproduced regularly and is used only before
important competitions, not for training." For other substances important to muscular
activity, such as ATP, concentrations "do not change substantially even after very hard
exercise," and restoration times for different substances vary by unknown amounts: "it is
absolutely unclear which criteria (substances) one should use for selecting proper time
intervals between consecutive workouts." Their conclusion: "In general, the theory of
supercompensation is too simple to be correct. Over the last few years it has lost much of
its popularity" (printed p. 12). (PDF pp. 20-21, 29-30, printed pp. 11-12, 20-21.)

**Why it works** — The theory's claimed mechanism (biochemical depletion, then
overshoot-restoration above baseline) is exactly what the authors say lacks experimental
support outside muscle glycogen; no independent mechanism is offered here beyond what the
theory itself claims and the authors then dispute.

**When to apply** — Inference: useful as a simple, visual model for explaining
workout-rest timing to an athlete or a junior coach, and as the conceptual basis some
coaches still use to schedule the final week before competition (see the coach-A/coach-B
tapering contrast in
[[principle--two-factor-fitness-fatigue-theory-and-training-effects-taxonomy]]). Not useful
as a basis for a specific, defensible rest-interval prescription, since the authors state
plainly that the substance(s) that should govern that interval are not known.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not cite "the supercompensation phase" as an experimentally
established phenomenon for training load broadly; the authors, writing this same textbook,
call the general theory unproven and "too simple to be correct" for most substances. This
is a stronger, more explicit critique than this library's existing Bompa entry
([[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]]), which frames supercompensation
descriptively (phase durations, Selye's GAS) and only notes in its "When NOT to apply" that
"contemporary sport science largely prefers" the two-factor model, without this book's
direct statement that the phase's existence is unproven for most substances. Confidence is
set `contested` here because the source itself argues against its own descriptive claim,
not because another library book disagrees with it (though Bompa's more favorable framing
is itself part of that contest — see Related for the reciprocal-link suggestion).

**Example** — The overloading microcycle (figure 1.6): three training sessions with short
rest intervals stack fatigue faster than it can clear, followed by one longer rest interval
timed so the next (fourth) workout coincides with the resulting supercompensation phase.
The authors present this as a popular coaching belief ("the common belief is that such a
training routine produces a final supercompensation that is greater than normal"), not as
their own endorsed or proven claim.

**Related** — [[principle--two-factor-fitness-fatigue-theory-and-training-effects-taxonomy]]
(the model the authors present as more sophisticated), 
[[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]] (reciprocal-link suggestion:
this book's explicit "unproven for most substances" critique is stronger evidence for that
entry's own brief caveat and could be cited there),
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]] (a
different book's competing model for the same critique, worth cross-referencing).

# The Two-Factor (Fitness-Fatigue) Theory, Training-Effect Taxonomy, and Its Tapering Payoff

**What it is** — The **two-factor theory** ("more sophisticated than the supercompensation
theory," printed p. 12) treats preparedness as not stable but varying with time, built from
two components: **physical fitness**, the slow-changing motor components of preparedness
(does not vary substantially over minutes, hours, or days), and **fatigue**, which can
change quickly from a workout, psychological overstress, or sudden illness. The immediate
effect of a workout is the combination of (a) fitness gain and (b) fatigue; their summation
determines the final outcome (figure 1.7, recovered here from the page image because the
OCR text drops the equation's subscripts and exponents):

Preparedness = P₀ + P₁e^(−t/k₁) − P₂e^(−t/k₂)

where P₀ is initial preparedness, P₁ is the fitness gain, P₂ is the fatigue effect
estimated immediately after the workout, t is time, k₁ and k₂ are time constants, and e is
the base of natural logarithms (≈2.718). The fitness gain from one session is moderate but
long-lasting; the fatigue effect is greater in magnitude but shorter in duration — "for most
crude estimations," the two differ by a factor of three: fatigue lasts about a third as
long, so a 24-hour fatigue impact implies the fitness trace persists through 72 hours

# Maximal Muscular Performance: Pm/Vm/Fm, Maximum Maximorum, and Parametric Relations

**What it is** — When an athlete performs a motor task (e.g. putting a shot) with maximal
effort across repeated attempts, the best single result is the individual's **maximal
muscular performance**, symbolized Pm (or Vm for maximal velocity, Fm for maximal force).
A **parameter** is an independent variable that is deliberately changed across attempts —
for instance, shot mass (the men's shot is 7,257 g, the women's 4,000 g). The **parametric
relation** describes how the dependent variables (Pm, Vm, Fm) change as that parameter is
systematically varied; between Vm and Fm it is typically **negative**: the greater the
force applied to the object, the lower its velocity, and vice versa (figure 2.1; 100
subjects, fast shoulder flexions with a barbell held, load 0-8 kg: velocity fell from
roughly 13 rad/s unloaded to under 4 rad/s at 8 kg. Data: Zatsiorsky, Smirnov & Kulik,
1969). The same negative (inverse) pattern holds across activities with different
parameters: cycling (gear ratio vs. pedaling frequency), rowing/kayaking (blade area vs.
blade velocity), uphill/downhill ambulation (slope vs. ambulation speed), throwing
(implement weight vs. release velocity), and the standing vertical jump (added/deduced
body weight vs. takeoff velocity) (printed p. 19, table). The **maximum maximorum**
performance (Pmm, Vmm, Fmm) is the single highest value achievable across all parameter
values — Vmm requires minimal resistance and short movement time (e.g. throwing light
objects, sprint dash); Fmm requires sufficiently high resistance. (PDF pp. 27-29, printed
pp. 18-20.)

**Why it works** — Inference: the parametric framework is a measurement convention, not a
physiological mechanism; it operationalizes the already-established inverse force-velocity
relationship (see
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]]
for the Hill-curve mechanism this book's own hyperbolic-equation section separately covers,
[[claim--rate-of-force-development-independent-of-maximal-force-and-explosive-strength-deficit]])
by fixing which variable is held constant (the task parameter) and which is measured, so
that a specific number (Pm at a specific parameter value) can be distinguished from the
single best-of-all-conditions number (Pmm).

**When to apply** — Use the Pm/Fm/Vm vs. Pmm/Fmm/Vmm distinction whenever comparing a
tested value (e.g. a force-plate reading at one load, one joint angle, one velocity) against
an athlete's true ceiling; a single test at one parameter value only measures Pm at that
parameter, not Pmm. **Eric's baseline:** this terminology (Fmm specifically) is the same
one the department's velocity-based 1RM estimation protocol implicitly works within — a
target mean velocity at 1RM is itself one point on a parametric force-velocity curve, not
Fmm (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment," citing
`ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md`).

**When NOT to apply** — Inference: do not treat a single-load force-plate or 1RM test
result as if it were Fmm; by this framework's own definition Fmm requires the test to find
the specific parameter value (resistance, joint angle, velocity) that elicits the highest
force, which a single standard test protocol does not systematically search for. This
chapter's terminology (Pm, Fm, Vm, Pmm, Fmm, Vmm) is this library's origin point for the
same Fmm/Vmm symbols already used, citing Zatsiorsky secondhand, in
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--types-of-maximal-strength]] and
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]];
this entry is the primary-source version of that terminology, not a duplicate of either.

**Example** — The gear-ratio example (printed p. 19, the authors' own): a coach who raises
a cyclist's gear ratio increases the force applied to the pedal but lowers pedaling
frequency (velocity) — a direct, mechanically obvious instance of the same negative
parametric relation shown for shot-putting.

**Related** — [[claim--strength-speed-correlation-depends-on-external-resistance]],
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--types-of-maximal-strength]] (reciprocal-link
suggestion: that entry cites Zatsiorsky's TFmax/CFmax/Fmm ladder secondhand; this entry is
the primary source for the Fmm/Vmm/Pmm terminology and could be linked from there),
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]].

# Whether Maximal Strength Correlates With Maximal Velocity Depends on the External Resistance

**What it is** — The **nonparametric relation** compares Fmm (or Fm) against Vm at a fixed
parameter value across different athletes — unlike the parametric relation (see
[[framework--maximal-muscular-performance-and-parametric-relations]]), nonparametric
relations are typically **positive**: stronger athletes tend to move a given resistance
faster. But the size of that correlation depends on how much resistance is involved. With a
meaningful load (6 kg dumbbell in the hand, n=100 shoulder flexions): angular velocity vs.
Fmm, R² = 0.522 (figure 2.2); with 8 kg load, R² = 0.692 (figure 2.12a). With **no load**
(near-Vmm conditions), the same population shows R² = 0.015 — "no significant correlation"
(figure 2.12b, printed p. 32). The authors state the scoped conclusion directly: "the
correlation between maximum maximorum values of Fmm and Vmm is 0: Stronger athletes are not
necessarily the fastest ones" (printed p. 20) — this claim is specifically about Fmm vs.
Vmm (near-zero resistance, e.g. an unloaded limb), not about force vs. velocity at
moderate-to-heavy resistance, where the correlation is positive and, for beginners
especially, often strong ("a positive correlation between Fmm and Vm is commonly
observed... especially true for beginning athletes," printed p. 20). The authors give
table tennis strokes (very light paddle, minimal resistance) as the clearest case where
"stronger athletes do not have an advantage" — a low- or near-zero-resistance task. (PDF
pp. 38-39, 49-50, printed pp. 20, 32.)

**Why it works** — Inference: as external resistance approaches zero, the task increasingly
tests pure movement velocity (a different motor ability) rather than force production
capacity, so an athlete's Fmm (built largely by resistance training) has progressively less
influence on the outcome; as resistance rises toward Fmm-relevant levels, the task
increasingly tests force capacity itself, so the correlation with Fmm should rise. The
authors state this pattern with data (R² rising from 0.015 at no load to 0.522-0.692 at
6-8 kg) but do not name the underlying neuromuscular mechanism (e.g. relative motor-unit
recruitment demand at each load) explicitly in this passage.

**When to apply** — Use this as the scoped, primary-source version of the "no
correlation between maximal strength and maximal velocity" claim already cited secondhand
in this library ([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]],
which marks that claim "contested by modern data (Wisloff et al. 2004... squat 1RM vs. 10 m
sprint time, r ~0.94)"). Reading this chapter directly shows Zatsiorsky's own claim was
always resistance-scoped (Fmm vs. Vmm specifically, near-zero external resistance), not a
blanket statement that strength and speed are uncorrelated at any load. A 10 m sprint
against bodyweight and ground reaction force is not a near-zero-resistance task the way an
unloaded arm swing or a table tennis stroke is; Inference: this does not resolve whether
Wisloff's squat-sprint correlation genuinely contradicts Zatsiorsky's claim, but it shows
the "contested" framing may rest on treating a narrowly-scoped claim as a general one — a
reviewer comparing the two should weigh how comparable sprinting's effective resistance is
to an unloaded-limb task before calling this a direct contradiction.

**When NOT to apply** — Inference: do not generalize "stronger athletes are not necessarily
faster" to all sport tasks; the data in this same chapter (R² = 0.522-0.692 at 6-8 kg load)
show the opposite at moderate resistance. The claim's true scope is near-zero-resistance
movement velocity specifically, and the correlation is also population-dependent: the text
notes beginners show a stronger Fmm-Vm relationship than elite/qualified athletes, whose
outcomes are more specific and less predictable from Fmm alone (printed p. 20; also see
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] on
transfer narrowing with sport mastery).

**Example** — A swim coach measuring a stroke-specific Fmm against swimming velocity
(printed p. 21, the authors' own worked example) finds the correlation significant, meaning
maximal-force training is worth the time investment for that stroke; had the correlation
been low, other qualities (muscular endurance, flexibility) would be the better target.
This illustrates the framework's practical use: test the correlation for the specific task
and resistance level in question rather than assuming an answer from a different task's
result.

[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]]
(reciprocal-link suggestion: cite this entry's resistance-dependent scoping as context for
that entry's "contested by Wisloff 2004" note),
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]].

# Explosive-Strength Deficit and Four Indices for Rate of Force Development

**What it is** — Peak force (Fm) takes time to develop: average time to peak isometric
force, Tm, is about 0.3-0.4 s, though the final 2-3% of the rise is disregarded in practice
because force output fluctuates near the top (figure 2.7). Most sport actions are far
shorter than that: sprint takeoff 0.08-0.10 s, long jump takeoff 0.11-0.12 s, high jump
takeoff 0.17-0.18 s, javelin delivery 0.16-0.18 s, shot put delivery 0.15-0.18 s, hand
takeoff in horse vaulting 0.18-0.21 s (printed p. 27, table). Because these motions are
shorter than Tm, Fmm cannot be reached during them; the gap between Fmm and the force
actually reached in a given short-duration condition (Fm) is the **explosive-strength
deficit (ESD)**: ESD (%) = 100(Fmm − Fm) / Fmm. In throwing delivery/takeoff phases, ESD is
typically about 50%: elite shot-putters' peak force in a throw (21.0 m throws) is about
50-60 kg, versus 220-240 kg (or 110-120 kg per arm) in a bench press Fmm — so throwers use
only about 50% of Fmm during the throw (printed p. 27). Four indices quantify explosive
strength and rate of force development from a force-time curve (figure 2.7's symbols): (a)
**Index of Explosive Strength (IES)** = Fm/Tm; (b) **Reactivity Coefficient (RC)** =
Fm/(TmW), W = athlete's weight, typically highly correlated with jumping performance,
especially post-takeoff body velocity; (c) **Force gradient (S-gradient)** = F0.5/T0.5
(F0.5 = half of Fm, T0.5 = time to reach it), characterizing rate of force development in
the early phase of effort; (d) **A-gradient** = F0.5/(Tmax − T0.5), quantifying rate of
force development in the late stage of an explosive effort. The authors state directly:
"Fm and the rate of force development, particularly the S-gradient, are not correlated.
Strong people do not necessarily possess a high rate of force development" (printed p. 28).
(PDF pp. 35-37, printed pp. 26-28.)

**Why it works** — Inference: peak force and rate of force development are governed by
different neuromuscular demands — reaching a high force ceiling depends on total motor-unit
recruitment and cross-sectional area, while rate of rise depends on how quickly that
recruitment and rate coding can be mobilized from rest, which the authors treat as a
partly-independent quality without stating the underlying mechanism explicitly in this
passage.

**When to apply** — As the direct primary-source statement, with a stated mechanism (time
availability in short-duration sport actions) and named indices, for why max-strength
testing alone under-informs explosive/short-ground-contact sports. This duplicates the
finding already in this library at
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]]
(there marked `proven` and cited without these specific formulas or the ESD/time-table
data); this entry adds the ESD definition, the four named indices (IES, RC, S-gradient,
A-gradient), and the elite-motion time-to-peak-force table the Supertraining entry does not
carry — a genuinely new angle worth cross-linking rather than a duplicate. **Eric's
baseline:** the department's ODSF force-plate framework already separates output, driver,
and strategy metrics rather than reporting peak force alone (`method-baseline.md`, "Force
plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing `hd-odsf-metrics.md`); Inference: RC and
S-gradient are concrete, formula-defined driver/strategy-type metrics this framework could
compute from existing force-plate time-series data, though neither source states that link.

**When NOT to apply** — Inference: ESD and the four indices are single-lab, Soviet-era
formalisms (not independently replicated in this ingest), so confidence stays `supported`,
not `proven`, despite the underlying force-time-curve concept being broadly accepted in
modern sport science. The time-to-peak-force table (0.08-0.21 s across events) is specific
to the cited elite populations and events; do not assume identical thresholds for other
sports or skill levels without separate verification.

**Example** — The two-athlete contrast (figure 2.9, the authors' own): Athlete A produces
higher force than Athlete B when the time available is short (in the "time-deficit zone"),
but B produces higher force when time is not limited. Training A's maximal strength would
not help A's performance if A's sport action stays inside the time-deficit zone — the
limiting factor there is explosive strength (rate of force development), not Fmm.

**Related** —
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]]
(reciprocal-link suggestion: cross-reference this entry's ESD formula, four indices, and
elite time-to-peak-force table as the primary-source detail behind that entry's citation),
[[framework--maximal-muscular-performance-and-parametric-relations]].

# Explosive-Strength Deficit and Four Indices for Rate of Force Development

**What it is** — Peak force (Fm) takes time to develop: average time to peak isometric
force, Tm, is about 0.3-0.4 s, though the final 2-3% of the rise is disregarded in practice
because force output fluctuates near the top (figure 2.7). Most sport actions are far
shorter than that: sprint takeoff 0.08-0.10 s, long jump takeoff 0.11-0.12 s, high jump
takeoff 0.17-0.18 s, javelin delivery 0.16-0.18 s, shot put delivery 0.15-0.18 s, hand
takeoff in horse vaulting 0.18-0.21 s (printed p. 27, table). Because these motions are
shorter than Tm, Fmm cannot be reached during them; the gap between Fmm and the force
actually reached in a given short-duration condition (Fm) is the **explosive-strength
deficit (ESD)**: ESD (%) = 100(Fmm − Fm) / Fmm. In throwing delivery/takeoff phases, ESD is
typically about 50%: elite shot-putters' peak force in a throw (21.0 m throws) is about
50-60 kg, versus 220-240 kg (or 110-120 kg per arm) in a bench press Fmm — so throwers use
only about 50% of Fmm during the throw (printed p. 27). Four indices quantify explosive
strength and rate of force development from a force-time curve (figure 2.7's symbols): (a)
**Index of Explosive Strength (IES)** = Fm/Tm; (b) **Reactivity Coefficient (RC)** =
Fm/(TmW), W = athlete's weight, typically highly correlated with jumping performance,
especially post-takeoff body velocity; (c) **Force gradient (S-gradient)** = F0.5/T0.5
(F0.5 = half of Fm, T0.5 = time to reach it), characterizing rate of force development in
the early phase of effort; (d) **A-gradient** = F0.5/(Tmax − T0.5), quantifying rate of
force development in the late stage of an explosive effort. The authors state directly:
"Fm and the rate of force development, particularly the S-gradient, are not correlated.
Strong people do not necessarily possess a high rate of force development" (printed p. 28).
(PDF pp. 35-37, printed pp. 26-28.)

**Why it works** — Inference: peak force and rate of force development are governed by
different neuromuscular demands — reaching a high force ceiling depends on total motor-unit
recruitment and cross-sectional area, while rate of rise depends on how quickly that
recruitment and rate coding can be mobilized from rest, which the authors treat as a
partly-independent quality without stating the underlying mechanism explicitly in this
passage.

**When to apply** — As the direct primary-source statement, with a stated mechanism (time
availability in short-duration sport actions) and named indices, for why max-strength
testing alone under-informs explosive/short-ground-contact sports. This duplicates the
finding already in this library at
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]]
(there marked `proven` and cited without these specific formulas or the ESD/time-table
data); this entry adds the ESD definition, the four named indices (IES, RC, S-gradient,
A-gradient), and the elite-motion time-to-peak-force table the Supertraining entry does not
carry — a genuinely new angle worth cross-linking rather than a duplicate. **Eric's
baseline:** the department's ODSF force-plate framework already separates output, driver,
and strategy metrics rather than reporting peak force alone (`method-baseline.md`, "Force
plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing `hd-odsf-metrics.md`); Inference: RC and
S-gradient are concrete, formula-defined driver/strategy-type metrics this framework could
compute from existing force-plate time-series data, though neither source states that link.

**When NOT to apply** — Inference: ESD and the four indices are single-lab, Soviet-era
formalisms (not independently replicated in this ingest), so confidence stays `supported`,
not `proven`, despite the underlying force-time-curve concept being broadly accepted in
modern sport science. The time-to-peak-force table (0.08-0.21 s across events) is specific
to the cited elite populations and events; do not assume identical thresholds for other
sports or skill levels without separate verification.

**Example** — The two-athlete contrast (figure 2.9, the authors' own): Athlete A produces
higher force than Athlete B when the time available is short (in the "time-deficit zone"),
but B produces higher force when time is not limited. Training A's maximal strength would
not help A's performance if A's sport action stays inside the time-deficit zone — the
limiting factor there is explosive strength (rate of force development), not Fmm.

[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]]
(reciprocal-link suggestion: cross-reference this entry's ESD formula, four indices, and
elite time-to-peak-force table as the primary-source detail behind that entry's citation),

# Maximal Muscular Performance: Pm/Vm/Fm, Maximum Maximorum, and Parametric Relations

**What it is** — When an athlete performs a motor task (e.g. putting a shot) with maximal
effort across repeated attempts, the best single result is the individual's **maximal
muscular performance**, symbolized Pm (or Vm for maximal velocity, Fm for maximal force).
A **parameter** is an independent variable that is deliberately changed across attempts —
for instance, shot mass (the men's shot is 7,257 g, the women's 4,000 g). The **parametric
relation** describes how the dependent variables (Pm, Vm, Fm) change as that parameter is
systematically varied; between Vm and Fm it is typically **negative**: the greater the
force applied to the object, the lower its velocity, and vice versa (figure 2.1; 100
subjects, fast shoulder flexions with a barbell held, load 0-8 kg: velocity fell from
roughly 13 rad/s unloaded to under 4 rad/s at 8 kg. Data: Zatsiorsky, Smirnov & Kulik,
1969). The same negative (inverse) pattern holds across activities with different
parameters: cycling (gear ratio vs. pedaling frequency), rowing/kayaking (blade area vs.
blade velocity), uphill/downhill ambulation (slope vs. ambulation speed), throwing
(implement weight vs. release velocity), and the standing vertical jump (added/deduced
body weight vs. takeoff velocity) (printed p. 19, table). The **maximum maximorum**
performance (Pmm, Vmm, Fmm) is the single highest value achievable across all parameter
values — Vmm requires minimal resistance and short movement time (e.g. throwing light
objects, sprint dash); Fmm requires sufficiently high resistance. (PDF pp. 27-29, printed
pp. 18-20.)

**Why it works** — Inference: the parametric framework is a measurement convention, not a
physiological mechanism; it operationalizes the already-established inverse force-velocity
relationship (see
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]]
for the Hill-curve mechanism this book's own hyperbolic-equation section separately covers,
[[claim--rate-of-force-development-independent-of-maximal-force-and-explosive-strength-deficit]])
by fixing which variable is held constant (the task parameter) and which is measured, so
that a specific number (Pm at a specific parameter value) can be distinguished from the
single best-of-all-conditions number (Pmm).

**When to apply** — Use the Pm/Fm/Vm vs. Pmm/Fmm/Vmm distinction whenever comparing a
tested value (e.g. a force-plate reading at one load, one joint angle, one velocity) against
an athlete's true ceiling; a single test at one parameter value only measures Pm at that
parameter, not Pmm. **Eric's baseline:** this terminology (Fmm specifically) is the same
one the department's velocity-based 1RM estimation protocol implicitly works within — a
target mean velocity at 1RM is itself one point on a parametric force-velocity curve, not
Fmm (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment," citing
`ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md`).

**When NOT to apply** — Inference: do not treat a single-load force-plate or 1RM test
result as if it were Fmm; by this framework's own definition Fmm requires the test to find
the specific parameter value (resistance, joint angle, velocity) that elicits the highest
force, which a single standard test protocol does not systematically search for. This
chapter's terminology (Pm, Fm, Vm, Pmm, Fmm, Vmm) is this library's origin point for the
same Fmm/Vmm symbols already used, citing Zatsiorsky secondhand, in
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--types-of-maximal-strength]] and
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]];
this entry is the primary-source version of that terminology, not a duplicate of either.

**Example** — The gear-ratio example (printed p. 19, the authors' own): a coach who raises
a cyclist's gear ratio increases the force applied to the pedal but lowers pedaling
frequency (velocity) — a direct, mechanically obvious instance of the same negative
parametric relation shown for shot-putting.

**Related** — [[claim--strength-speed-correlation-depends-on-external-resistance]],
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--types-of-maximal-strength]] (reciprocal-link
suggestion: that entry cites Zatsiorsky's TFmax/CFmax/Fmm ladder secondhand; this entry is
the primary source for the Fmm/Vmm/Pmm terminology and could be linked from there),
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]].

# Eccentric Force Can Exceed Isometric Strength by 50-100%, Which Raises Injury Risk

**What it is** — Force in the yielding (eccentric/plyometric) phase of a motion "can easily
exceed the maximal isometric strength of an athlete by 50 to 100%," and the same holds true
for isolated muscles, where "the eccentric force for a single muscle may reach a level of
up to twice the zero velocity (isometric) force" (printed p. 33). Eccentric forces rise
substantially with initial increases in joint movement velocity, then remain essentially
constant with further velocity increases (figure 2.14) — mainly true for qualified
athletes and multijoint motions such as leg extension; the authors separately note that in
untrained persons, per "recently published data," maximal voluntary eccentric knee
extension/flexion torque is independent of movement velocity and stays at an isometric
level. If the same external force is developed both concentrically and eccentrically, fewer
muscle fibers are activated eccentrically, so EMG activity is lower in eccentric actions
than concentric ones at matched force (printed p. 34). A worked example: the maximal
isometric grip force of male weightlifters, measured with a dynamometer, is typically under
1,000 N; an athlete lifting a 250-kg barbell applies a maximal instantaneous force of "well
over 4,000 N" to the bar, meaning roughly 2,000 N per arm — double the grip dynamometer
ceiling — yet the athlete sustains the lift "without extending the grip" (printed p. 34).
Because eccentric exercises involve high force development, injury risk is elevated even
when the eccentric force is submaximal; downhill running is given as an example that can
"easily induce delayed muscle soreness, especially in unprepared athletes," caused by
damaged muscle fibers, though "a small magnitude of the damage is considered by some
experts a normal precursor to the adaptation of muscle to increased use." Conditioning
muscle reduces injury amount (printed p. 34). (PDF pp. 43-44, printed pp. 34-35.)

**Why it works** — Inference: the authors do not state the cross-bridge/sliding-filament
mechanism for why eccentric actions produce higher force at lower metabolic/neural cost
(fewer active fibers per given force) in this passage; this is consistent with, but not
explained by, the force-velocity relationship covered elsewhere in this chapter (see
[[framework--maximal-muscular-performance-and-parametric-relations]]) and in this library's
Supertraining entries on muscle mechanics.

**When to apply** — As a quantified, citable rationale for treating eccentric loading
(downhill running, eccentric-emphasis lifting, drop landings) as a distinct injury-risk
category requiring its own progression, separate from concentric/isometric strength
qualification. Inference: the grip-strength example is a useful coaching illustration that
an athlete's ability to sustain a lift does not require the grip muscles to be working
maximally in the sense a dynamometer test would show, since the mechanical demand (holding
position under eccentric-capable tension) differs from a maximal concentric or isometric
grip effort.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single-textbook synthesis citing unnamed "recently
published data" for the untrained-eccentric-velocity-independence claim (printed p. 34);
treat the 50-100% and "up to twice" figures as the range the authors report, not as a fixed
individual multiplier — do not compute a specific athlete's eccentric capacity as exactly
1.5-2.0x their tested isometric max without direct eccentric testing. Inference: "a small
magnitude of damage... a normal precursor to adaptation" is reported as some experts'
view, not the authors' own asserted mechanism; do not treat controlled muscle damage as a
required or recommended training stimulus on this text's authority alone.

**Example** — Downhill running as unprepared-athlete DOMS trigger (printed p. 34, the
authors' own example): even without near-maximal eccentric force, repeated eccentric
loading in an athlete not conditioned to it produces delayed soreness from fiber damage,
illustrating that "not maximal" does not mean "not risky" for eccentric work specifically.

**Related** — [[framework--stretch-shortening-cycle-mechanisms-and-tendon-elastic-storage]]
(the SSC's use of this same elevated eccentric force capacity),
[[framework--maximal-muscular-performance-and-parametric-relations]].

# Four Reasons the Stretch-Shortening Cycle Increases Force, and Why Elite Athletes Store Energy in Tendons

**What it is** — If a muscle shortens immediately after being stretched (the
stretch-shortening cycle, SSC, "reversible muscular action"), force and power output
increase and energy expenditure decreases versus a shortening-only (concentric) action. The
authors give four reasons for the increased force in the shortening phase: (1) at the peak
of the cycle (the lengthening-to-shortening transition), force is developed under
isometric-like conditions, so Fmm rather than the lower, velocity-limited Fm is exerted;
(2) because force begins rising during the eccentric phase, the time available for force
development is longer than in a pure concentric effort — countermovement jumps, not drop
jumps, are given as the authors' example of this mechanism; (3) **peripheral** (muscle and
tendon elasticity): stretched muscle or tendon stores elastic (strain) energy proportional
to the applied force and the induced deformation, which is recoiled during the concentric
phase (figure 2.16: stiffer bodies store less energy per unit force, more compliant bodies
store more, for the same force); and (4) **central** (neural/reflex): the myotatic
(stretch) reflex adds a positive, force-increasing contribution from spindle discharge
during stretch, while the Golgi tendon reflex adds a negative (inhibitory) contribution
that limits force when tension rises sharply — the net SSC force enhancement is the
combination of a muscle-tendon-elasticity component and these two opposing
length-feedback/force-feedback neural components (figure 2.18, from Houk 1974 via Komi
1986). Tendon stiffness is constant; muscle stiffness varies with the force exerted — the
more tension, the stiffer the active muscle. In elite athletes the active muscle's
stiffness can exceed the tendon's stiffness, meaning the tendon deforms more than the
muscle under load and so stores most of the elastic energy — the authors note fast-running
animals such as horses have "short, strong muscles and lengthy, compliant tendons" that
"work as springs" for exactly this reason (figure 2.17, printed p. 35). (PDF pp. 44-46,
printed pp. 34-36, 38.)

**Why it works** — The authors state the mechanism directly across the four listed reasons
(force-time history, elastic energy storage, and the myotatic/Golgi neural interplay), so
this is the source's own stated mechanism rather than this entry's inference, except where
marked.

**When to apply** — As the mechanistic basis for why plyometric/reactive training targets a
different quality than either pure concentric strength training or static flexibility work
(see [[claim--eccentric-force-exceeds-concentric-and-isometric-force]] for the elevated
eccentric force capacity this cycle exploits, and
[[claim--reversible-muscular-action-is-a-trainable-skill-not-automatic]] for why this
capacity does not transfer automatically from heavy lifting). Inference: the muscle-vs-tendon
stiffness relationship (figure 2.17) supports why tendon stiffness/compliance, not just
muscle strength, is a relevant training target for reactive-strength qualities in elite
athletes specifically.

**When NOT to apply** — Inference: the four-reason breakdown is presented as the authors'
synthesis of separately-cited mechanisms (Komi 1986 for the neural figure; general
elasticity physics for figures 2.16-2.17), not as a single unified, independently-tested
model; treat each of the four contributions as separately-supported components rather than
a fully integrated, quantitatively-partitioned account of SSC force enhancement. Do not
assume the horse-tendon analogy transfers quantitatively to human athletic populations; it
is offered as an illustrative comparison, not a measured human finding.

**Example** — The authors' own comparison: countermovement jumps are evidence of the
first mechanism (force developed isometrically at the stretch-shorten transition, and a
longer available time for force development than a static-start jump) — this is why
squat-jump (static start) performance and countermovement-jump performance are trained and
interpreted as distinct qualities, consistent with force-plate practice that runs both
variants separately.

**Related** — [[claim--eccentric-force-exceeds-concentric-and-isometric-force]],
[[claim--reversible-muscular-action-is-a-trainable-skill-not-automatic]],
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]]
(reciprocal-link suggestion: that entry's SEC/PEC muscle model is the finer-grained
anatomical account of the same elastic-energy storage this entry describes at the
muscle-vs-tendon level; worth cross-referencing both ways),
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]] (the
static-vs-countermovement jump comparison this entry's mechanism (1) underlies).

# Reversible Muscular Action (SSC Skill) Must Be Specifically Trained, Not Assumed From Strength

**What it is** — Reversible muscular action (using the stretch-shortening cycle
effectively) is innate to some movements (e.g. running takeoffs, "a spring in the leg")
but must be learned for others, such as throwing. Because many sport movements are complex
and executed briefly, "even some elite athletes fail to perform this reversible muscular
action correctly" (printed p. 35). The authors state that before 1960, SSC training was
accidental — improvement was a byproduct of other exercises; only since drop jumps and
similar exercises were incorporated into training has SSC capacity been trained
deliberately (they note the training method "has been erroneously called plyometrics by
some," since the reversible, not strictly eccentric, muscular action is the actual training
objective). The direct claim: "maximal muscular strength (Fmm) and forces produced in fast
reversible muscular action (Fm) are not correlated in good athletes and should be treated,
and trained, as separate motor abilities" — as evidence, "even world-class weightlifters
cannot compete with triple jumpers in drop jumping" because, absent specific training, the
Golgi tendon reflex inhibits extensor activity during landing even in very strong athletes,
capping how much force they can sustain without a compensating drop in output; specific
training inhibits that reflex, letting a trained athlete sustain high landing forces without
a force decrease, which is also why dropping height can then be increased. In beginners,
performance in SSC-type exercises can be improved through other exercises such as heavy
weightlifting; in qualified athletes, "this skill is very specific" and drop-jump
performance does not improve from usual strength exercising alone, even with heavy weights
(figure 2.19, comparing 24 weeks of heavy-resistance vs. explosive/power training on
drop-jump height by dropping height: Hakkinen & Komi 1985). (PDF pp. 47-48, printed pp.
38-39.)

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is neural: the Golgi tendon reflex normally
inhibits extensor muscle activity when tension rises sharply during landing, protecting the
muscle-tendon unit; specific SSC/drop-jump training desensitizes or inhibits that reflex
response so the athlete can sustain higher landing forces without the reflex-driven force
drop. This is the authors' own stated mechanism, not this entry's inference.

**When to apply** — As direct justification for programming drop jumps, depth jumps, or
other SSC-specific exercises as their own training category, separate from and not
substitutable by heavy strength training, once an athlete is past the beginner stage where
general strength work still transfers. **Eric's baseline:** training time is deliberately
weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements including jumps
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.13`; `week1-lecture.md p.31`); Inference: this
claim supports keeping jump/SSC-specific work in the program as its own category for
qualified athletes rather than assuming continued heavy-strength gains will carry over to
reactive/SSC qualities.

**When NOT to apply** — Inference: the 1960-pre/post historical claim about accidental vs.
deliberate SSC training is presented without a specific citation in this passage; treat it
as the authors' historical framing, not a verified dated fact. The figure 2.19
Hakkinen-and-Komi comparison is cited as supporting evidence but is a single study (n=11
heavy-resistance group, n=10 explosive-training group); do not treat "heavy strength
training does not improve drop-jump performance in qualified athletes" as settled beyond
this cited study's population and protocol. Do not use "even world-class weightlifters
cannot compete with triple jumpers in drop jumping" to argue that strength training has no
value for reactive-strength athletes generally — the claim is about specific-skill
transfer, not about strength training's value for other qualities that also support jump
performance (peak force capacity, injury resilience).

**Example** — The authors' own contrast: a beginner's drop-jump-type performance can still
improve from general heavy weightlifting (transfer exists at low training age), but a
qualified athlete's drop-jump performance requires drop-jump-specific training and does not
improve further from added heavy-resistance work alone (figure 2.19a vs. 2.19b).

**Related** — [[framework--stretch-shortening-cycle-mechanisms-and-tendon-elastic-storage]],
[[claim--eccentric-force-exceeds-concentric-and-isometric-force]],
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]].

# Joint Strength Curves, Sticking Points, and the Moment-Arm Transformation to End-Point Force

**What it is** — A **strength curve** plots the external force (or moment of force) an
athlete can exert at a given motion against body posture/joint angle. Fmm is a function of
muscular force that undergoes two transformations: muscle-tendon force → joint moment
(torque, M = Fd, where d is the moment arm) → external end-point force (strength). Single-
joint strength curves take three general shapes: ascending, descending, or concave (figure
2.21). Worked examples (Zatsiorsky & Raitsin, 1973; n=24): elbow flexion strength peaks
near 90° (about 100% of Fmm) and falls to roughly 46-50% near full extension/flexion
(figure 2.22a); shoulder flexion strength is highest with the arm slightly behind the trunk
(around −30°, ~100%) and falls to about 37% at 150° (figure 2.22b). The weakest position in
a joint's range is the **sticking point**: the heaviest weight liftable through a full
range of motion cannot exceed the strength at the sticking point, even though other
positions in the range are stronger. Muscle length itself changes tension via two factors:
overlapping actin/myosin cross-bridge availability, and the contribution of elastic
(mainly parallel elastic) components — as a general rule (with a few exceptions, e.g. the
rectus femoris in some cyclists) muscles exert smaller tension at smaller lengths and higher
tension when stretched. Moment arm also changes with joint angle: the text's own example is
the biceps brachii (long head), whose moment arm was 11.5 mm at 180° (full extension) and
45.5 mm at 90° (elbow flexion) — a fourfold difference — meaning that if muscle tension
were identical at both angles, the moment of force (and thus external strength) would
change fourfold purely from the moment-arm change (printed p. 43, figure 2.24). For
two-joint muscles (e.g. gastrocnemius), Fmm at one joint depends on the angular position of
the *other* joint the muscle crosses: when the knee is maximally flexed and the ankle
plantarflexed, the shortened gastrocnemius cannot produce active plantar-flexion force — a
position usable for selectively training the soleus instead. (PDF pp. 49-54, printed pp.
40-44.)

**Why it works** — The mechanism is explicitly two-part and stated directly by the authors:
(1) muscle tension varies with muscle length (cross-bridge overlap plus elastic-component
contribution), and (2) the moment arm of that muscle force varies with joint angle
independent of tension itself; strength at any joint angle is their product (figure 2.24: a
muscle tension-angle curve × a moment-arm-angle curve = the resulting joint torque curve).

**When to apply** — As a quantified, citable rationale for coaching cues about
range-specific loading and for anticipating where in a lift's range an athlete will be
weakest (the sticking point), useful for accommodating-resistance programming (bands,
chains) or partial-range strength work targeted at a known sticking point. **Eric's
baseline:** this complements, rather than duplicates,
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique]]
(bar-path/torque-minimization coaching cues) and
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--joint-angle-and-limb-position-changes-force-output]]
(a separate set of joint-angle findings, e.g. forearm pronation, trunk flexion, head tilt,
from later in Supertraining); this entry supplies the moment-arm mechanism (the
11.5-to-45.5-mm biceps example, fourfold difference) underlying why those position effects
occur, which neither Supertraining entry itself derives from the muscle-length/moment-arm
product shown here.

**When NOT to apply** — Inference: the specific curve shapes and percentages (elbow flexion
peak ~90°, shoulder flexion peak near −30°, the 11.5/45.5 mm biceps figures) are
single-study data (Zatsiorsky & Raitsin, 1973 and 1992) from a specific population (n=24);
do not assume they transfer exactly to a different joint, muscle, or population without
verification. The rectus femoris exception (higher tension at shorter length, in some
cyclists) is noted as an exception to the general muscle-length rule, not a contradiction of
it — do not overgeneralize either the rule or its exception.

**Example** — The pull-up supination example (printed p. 44, the authors' own): gymnasts
performing pull-ups on rings always supinate the arms while flexing the elbows, though
nobody teaches them to; the movement pattern is simply more mechanically convenient. This
illustrates athletes self-organizing technique to work with, not against, their own joint
strength curves and moment-arm geometry (see
[[heuristic--athletes-self-organize-technique-to-minimize-secondary-moments]] for the

# Five Types of Mechanical Resistance, and Why Equipment Choice Can Break Sport-Movement Specificity

**What it is** — Resistance training equipment can be classified by the physical law
governing the resistance it provides: **elasticity** (F = k₁D; force proportional to
displacement/deformation D, coefficient k₁ = stiffness — springs, stretch cords, rubber
bands; force is greatest at the end of range, when deformation is largest); **inertia**
(Newton's second law, F = ma; force proportional to the mass being accelerated — hard to
isolate purely inertial resistance outside lab devices like an inertia wheel, since gravity
and friction intrude); **weight** (F = W + ma, W = object weight, a = vertical
acceleration); **hydrodynamic resistance** (F = k₂V², proportional to velocity squared —
swimming, rowing, kayaking); and **viscosity-based resistance** (F = k₃V, proportional to
velocity, k₃ = a coefficient — used in machines substituting for water-sport dryland
training). Exercises are also classified by whether they have **mechanical feedback**: in a
paddling stroke, higher muscular force raises oar velocity, which raises water resistance,
which in turn demands more muscular force (a closed loop, figure 2.4) — most sport
movements have this feedback loop. Mechanical feedback is **absent** specifically in
isometric exercise and with isokinetic devices (constant velocity regardless of force
applied), which is why those modes do not reproduce most sport movements' natural
force-resistance interaction. (PDF pp. 30-31, 33-34, 51-52, printed pp. 21, 23-24, 42-43.)

**Why it works** — Inference: because different sport movements are naturally resisted by
different physical laws (hydrodynamic for swimming, elastic/momentum-based for most
throwing and jumping, weight-and-inertia for lifting), an exercise's resistance type
determines how closely its force-velocity demand matches the target movement, independent
of which muscles it uses — this is the authors' own point in the dryland-training case
study below, though the general "resistance type governs specificity" framing is this
entry's synthesis of the mechanics they lay out.

**When to apply** — As a checklist when selecting resistance training equipment intended to
transfer to a specific sport skill: match the resistance-type profile (elastic, inertial,
weight-based, hydrodynamic, viscosity-based) to the target movement's actual resistance
type, not just its visible muscle groups or general movement pattern. This complements
[[framework--transfer-of-training-coefficient-calculation]] (Chapter 1) by giving a
mechanical reason, in addition to a measured-transfer-coefficient reason, that an exercise
might fail to transfer.

**When NOT to apply** — Inference: this is a mechanics-based classification, not itself a
ranked hierarchy of "better" and "worse" resistance types; each type is appropriate for
different training goals (elastic resistance for end-range loading, isokinetic/isometric
for eliminating the confound of a changing external load during rehab-style force testing,
despite lacking mechanical feedback). Do not treat "lacks mechanical feedback" as
disqualifying isometric or isokinetic training outright; the authors present it as a
descriptive difference from most sport movements, not a stated flaw.

**Example** — The authors' own case study, "Selection of Dryland Exercises for Swimmers"
(printed p. 25): a swim coach trialed extensible rubber bands (elastic resistance, pulling
force increased through the pull, unlike the customary stroke), a weightlifting pulley
machine (near-constant resistance across the pull, but the athletes could not relax at the
end of motion, unlike a real stroke), and friction/hydrodynamic training devices (either
constant resistance or resistance proportional to pull velocity, both meant to mimic water
resistance) — none matched the true stroke's resistance profile (proportional to the
squared hand velocity relative to water) exactly, illustrating why matching a device's
underlying resistance law to the sport movement's own is harder than it looks, even when
targeting the same muscle groups and general movement pattern.

**Related** — [[framework--transfer-of-training-coefficient-calculation]],
[[claim--strength-speed-correlation-depends-on-external-resistance]].

# Five Types of Mechanical Resistance, and Why Equipment Choice Can Break Sport-Movement Specificity

**What it is** — Resistance training equipment can be classified by the physical law

isolate purely inertial resistance outside lab devices like an inertia wheel, since gravity
and friction intrude); **weight** (F = W + ma, W = object weight, a = vertical
acceleration); **hydrodynamic resistance** (F = k₂V², proportional to velocity squared —
